seo.title: AI Crawler User Agents: The 2026 List for robots.txt
seo.meta_description: AI crawler user agents list: GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Meta and CCBot, and which to allow.

h1: AI Crawler User Agents: Which Bots to Allow and Which to Block
answer: The main AI crawler user agents are OpenAI's GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User; Anthropic's ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User; PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User; Google-Extended; Applebot-Extended; Meta-ExternalAgent; and Common Crawl's CCBot. Allow the search bots if you want to be cited; blocking training bots is a separate choice.
key_takeaways: Most AI companies separate search bots from training bots.
Blocking a search bot removes you from that platform's answers.
Blocking a training bot does not remove you from search answers.
Google-Extended does not affect Google Search or AI Overviews.
Check firewalls too: robots.txt is only part of access.

sections.heading: Why the user agent matters
sections.body_html: A user agent is the name a crawler gives when it requests a page. robots.txt rules are written per user agent, so knowing the exact names lets you decide, platform by platform, whether your content can be used for AI search answers, for model training, or both. Getting a name wrong means your rule does nothing, or blocks something you meant to allow.

sections.heading: OpenAI
sections.body_html:
• OAI-SearchBot: finds pages to show and link in ChatGPT search results. Allow it if you want to appear in ChatGPT answers.
  • ChatGPT-User: fetches a page when a ChatGPT user or custom GPT asks for it.
  • GPTBot: collects content that may be used to train OpenAI's models. Blocking it does not remove you from ChatGPT search results, according to OpenAI.

sections.heading: Anthropic and Perplexity
sections.body_html:
Anthropic lists three bots: ClaudeBot for training data, Claude-SearchBot for improving search results in Claude, and Claude-User for fetching pages when a Claude user asks. Anthropic says its bots respect robots.txt.

Perplexity uses PerplexityBot to surface and link sites in its search results, and says it is not used to crawl content for training foundation models. Perplexity-User fetches pages in response to a user's question.

sections.heading: Google, Apple and Meta
sections.body_html:
Google-Extended is a control token, not a separate crawler: it tells Google whether content crawled by Googlebot may be used to train Gemini models and for grounding in some Gemini features. Google says it does not affect inclusion or ranking in Google Search, including AI Overviews.

Apple uses Applebot for Siri, Spotlight and Safari features. Applebot-Extended lets publishers opt out of their content being used to train Apple's generative foundation models; Apple notes Applebot may still crawl pages for its other features.

Meta lists Meta-ExternalAgent, which crawls for uses such as training AI models or improving products by indexing content, and Meta-ExternalFetcher, which fetches individual links at a user's request.

sections.heading: Common Crawl
sections.body_html: CCBot is the crawler of Common Crawl, a non-profit that publishes a large open web archive used widely in research and AI training. Common Crawl documents a robots.txt rule to block it and warns that some crawlers falsely identify themselves as CCBot, so it recommends verifying user agents.

For a business that wants leads from AI search, the usual choice is to allow every search and user-fetch bot. Whether to allow training bots is a policy decision; allowing them may help models learn about your brand over time.

sections.heading: An example robots.txt
sections.body_html:
This example allows AI search, blocks two training crawlers and keeps a private folder closed to all bots:

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Bots not named in their own group follow the * rules, so OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot are allowed here. Each crawler follows the most specific group that matches its name.

sections.heading: Check more than robots.txt
sections.body_html:
1. Firewalls and CDNs may block AI bots by default; check their bot settings.
  2. Server logs show which bots actually reach you and their response codes.
  3. Verify identities: several companies publish IP ranges so you can confirm a bot is genuine.
  4. Review quarterly: companies add and rename crawlers, so revisit the official documentation.

sections.heading: How to verify a bot is genuine
sections.body_html:
Anyone can put "GPTBot" or "ClaudeBot" in a request header, so a user agent name alone proves nothing. Before you whitelist or block traffic based on it, confirm the request really comes from the company it claims. OpenAI and Perplexity publish the IP ranges their crawlers use, and Common Crawl says CCBot now runs from dedicated IP ranges. For Googlebot and Bingbot, the standard method is a reverse DNS lookup on the requesting IP, followed by a forward lookup to confirm it resolves back.

Many CDNs and security services can do this automatically and label verified bots. If yours offers a verified-bot category, use it instead of matching names yourself.

sections.heading: Mistakes we see most often
sections.body_html:
• Blocking every AI bot with one rule, which also removes the site from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity answers.
  • Misspelled user agents, such as "GPT-Bot" or "Claude-Web", that match nothing.
  • Relying on robots.txt while a firewall blocks the bot anyway, so the allow rule never matters.
  • Blocking Google-Extended to stay out of AI Overviews, which it does not do.
  • Never re-checking: crawler names and purposes change, so a rule written in 2024 may no longer do what you intended.

A quarterly review of robots.txt, firewall settings and server logs catches nearly all of these.

faqs.q: What are the main AI crawler user agents?
faqs.a: GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User (OpenAI); ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User (Anthropic); PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User; Google-Extended; Applebot-Extended; Meta-ExternalAgent; and CCBot.
Blocking GPTBot stops OpenAI using your content for training but, according to OpenAI, does not remove you from ChatGPT search results, which use OAI-SearchBot.

faqs.q: Does blocking Google-Extended remove me from AI Overviews?
faqs.a: No. Google says Google-Extended does not affect inclusion or ranking in Google Search, including AI Overviews.

faqs.q: Which AI bots should a business allow?
faqs.a: If you want leads from AI search, allow the search and user-fetch bots: OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User, PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User, Googlebot and Bingbot.

faqs.q: How do I know which AI bots visit my site?
faqs.a: Check your server or CDN logs for their user agent names, and verify them against the IP ranges each company publishes.

faqs.q: Can fake bots pretend to be AI crawlers?
faqs.a: Yes. Common Crawl warns that some crawlers falsely identify as CCBot. Verify by IP range where the company publishes one.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Google, Apple and Common Crawl all document robots.txt controls for their crawlers. Bots that fake their identity may not, which is why verifying by IP range or reverse DNS matters for anything you want to enforce strictly.
